title: Phantom churners
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  Phantom churners
  
    My churn model scored an AUC of 0.79 and ranked customers beautifully. It also
    predicted that 12,180 of 30,000 subscribers were about to leave, in a market where the
    real number was closer to 700. Both things were true at once — and only one of them mattered for
    the budget.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseTelecom churn & retention economics
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm · XGBoost
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The assignment
    A Singapore mobile carrier wanted to know which retention programs to fund. The chain of
    reasoning is standard: predict who will churn, work out which interventions move that number,
    convert the movement into lifetime value, and set a budget from there.
    Every step after the first depends on the model producing a probability, not
    just a ranking. That distinction is the whole story here.
  

  
    Picking a model
    I compared logistic regression against two tree ensembles on a 39,000-row training sample,
    using log transforms on the skewed spend and usage variables:
  

  
    



Model
AUC
Note

XGBoost (tuned)

    Tuned XGBoost won on test AUC and held its shape between train and test on the gains curves.
    A defensible choice, and by every metric I had been taught to check, a finished model.
  

  
    Then I looked at the level
    Applying that model to the 30,000-customer representative sample — the one built to mirror the
    actual subscriber base — produced a mean predicted churn probability of 40.6%.
    The real market rate is about 2%.
  

  
    0.793Test AUC — genuinely good ranking
    40.6%Mean predicted churn
    ~2%Actual market churn
    17×Overstatement of churners
  

  
    The cause was in the training data. The 39,000-row sample had been built at roughly
    50% churn — deliberately oversampled so the models would have enough positive
    cases to learn from. That is a sensible thing to do for estimation, and a catastrophic thing to
    forget afterwards. The model learned the shape of churn risk on a world where half of everyone
    leaves, then reported those probabilities into a world where one in fifty does.
    The fix was to re-estimate on the full million-row dataset, which carries the true ~2% base
    rate — same features, same hyperparameters, no retuning. About 682,000 training rows.
  

  
    
      
        Mean predicted churn on the 30,000-customer representative sample
        Identical model specification. The only change is the base rate of the
        data it was fitted on.
      
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Trained on
Churn in training data
Mean predicted churn
Implied churners




39K sample
~50%
40.60%
12,180


1M dataset
~2%
2.38%
713




    
  

  
    Retrained, the same architecture returned a test AUC of 0.794 — statistically
    indistinguishable from the 0.793 I started with. The ranking never changed. The number attached to
    each customer changed by a factor of seventeen.

    
      AUC only asks whether riskier customers score higher than safer ones. It is unchanged by any
      transformation that preserves order — so a model can be perfectly ranked and
      arbitrarily mis-scaled, and no ranking metric will ever tell you. Lifetime value
      calculations use the level, not the order. Had I shipped the first model, every budget
      downstream would have been inflated seventeenfold.
    
  

  
    Testing five retention programs
    With probabilities on the right scale, I simulated five interventions by editing the input that
    each program targets — set overage charges to zero, set retention calls to zero — and re-scoring
    through the model.
  

  
    
      
        Observed churn versus predicted churn after intervention
        Each pair is one program, on the customers who would receive it. Hover
        any row for detail.
      
      
        All five
        Funded only
      
    
    
      Observed churn in group
      Predicted after intervention
      Sample mean prediction, 2.38%
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Program
Targeted
Observed churn
Predicted after
Funded






    
  

  
    Read at face value, two programs made things worse — customer care and early-tenure engagement
    both showed higher churn after the simulated fix. The notebook I wrote at the time put this down
    to "how XGBoost combines things" and dropped them.

    
      That conclusion doesn't hold, and the error is mine. The two numbers in each
      pair aren't comparable. Observed churn is what actually happened to those customers.
      Predicted after is what the model says post-intervention. To isolate an intervention
      effect you have to compare the model's prediction before against its prediction
      after — same model, same customers, one variable changed. I never computed the
      before.
      New Handset Support proves the point. Its 26 customers contain zero actual churners, so
      observed churn is 0.0% — and against zero, any positive prediction looks like the program
      causes churn. That isn't an intervention effect. It's a 26-person sample with no events in it.
    

    So the honest statement is not "two programs backfired." It is that the sign of the
    effect is unknown for four of the five, because the baseline was never measured. Only
    Usage-Based Plan is safe, and only because its gap is wide enough to survive the confusion.
    There's a second inconsistency I found on re-reading: First Call Resolution shows the largest
    apparent improvement of any service program — 3.32% down to 2.38% — and it was dropped from the
    economics anyway, while New Handset Support, which looks worse on the same flawed comparison, was
    kept. Neither decision follows from the numbers.
  

  
    The economics that survived
    For the programs that went forward, I valued each over a 60-month window, discounting at 10% a
    year. Breakeven is the most you could spend per customer before the retained revenue stops
    covering it; I proposed half that, as a margin against the effect being smaller than modeled.

  Figures in Singapore dollars. "Total budget" is proposed spend per customer × customers
  targeted — an investment ceiling, not a profit forecast.

  
    One caveat belongs in the open rather than a footnote: the Student Bundle's S$452 breakeven does
    not come from the model at all. Occupation is categorical, so I couldn't simulate it the way I
    simulated overage. The 1.5% churn reduction behind that number is an assumption I
    chose. It happens to produce the highest breakeven in the table, which is exactly the
    situation where an assumption deserves to be labelled loudly.
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    Why oversampling breaks probabilities but not rankings
    
    With ~2% churn, a 39,000-row sample holds only about 800 churners. Oversampling to 50/50 gives
    the model far more signal per unit of compute, which is why it's standard practice for rare events.
    What it changes is the intercept. The model learns P(churn | features) under a prior of 0.5 and
    reports that, even though the deployment prior is 0.02. Because the distortion is monotone, every
    rank-based diagnostic — AUC, gains, lift — is untouched. Every level-based use — expected churners,
    lifetime value, budgets — is wrong by roughly the ratio of the two priors.
    Two fixes exist. Re-estimate on data carrying the true base rate, which is what I did. Or keep
    the oversampled fit and correct the intercept analytically. Worth noting: the weighted logistic
    regression came out correctly scaled at 2.29% on the same sample, because the weights restored the
    prior. The tree ensemble had no such correction, and I didn't add one.
    
    

    
    What "simulating an intervention" actually assumes
    
    Setting overage = 0 and re-scoring is a convenient move that smuggles in two strong
    assumptions.
    First, that the program works perfectly. Moving someone to a better-fitting plan
    is modeled as overage vanishing entirely, not shrinking. Real programs have partial take-up and
    partial effect.
    Second, and more seriously, that the association is causal. XGBoost learned that
    customers with overage churn more. It cannot distinguish "overage charges cause people to leave"
    from "the kind of customer who overruns their plan is also the kind who leaves." Zeroing the
    variable answers a question about the model, not about the world.
    This is why the case asks for a randomized trial design alongside the simulation, and why my
    proposal was to split the target group 50/50 and measure churn at 30 days and at 3–6 months. The
    model estimate is a prior for sizing the pilot — not a substitute for it.
    
    

    
    How lifetime value was computed
    
    For each targeted customer I projected monthly margin over 60 months, with survival to each month
    driven by the predicted churn probability, discounted at 10% annually. Running it twice — once at
    baseline churn, once at post-intervention churn — gives two lifetime values, and the difference is
    the value the program creates.
    Breakeven per customer is that difference. Spend exactly it and you are indifferent; spend less
    and you profit. The proposed figure is 50% of breakeven, which is a judgment call rather than a
    derived quantity, chosen because the effect estimates carry the uncertainty described above.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Compute the baseline prediction per group. This is the one real defect in the
    analysis. One extra line — the mean of the baseline prediction restricted to each target group —
    turns five ambiguous comparisons into five valid ones, and would likely change which programs got
    funded.
    Check calibration deliberately, not accidentally. I caught the 17× error because
    the mean prediction looked implausible. That is luck, not method. A calibration plot alongside every
    AUC would have surfaced it immediately, and I now treat "what is the mean predicted probability, and
    does it match the base rate?" as a required check before any model touches money.
    Drop the 26-customer program. New Handset Support cannot support any conclusion
    at that sample size. Reporting it as a S$0 breakeven implies a finding of "no value," when the honest
    statement is "no evidence either way."
    Put a range on the lifetime values. A 60-month projection compounds the churn
    estimate sixty times. Small errors in the probability become large errors in the total, and a single
    point estimate hides that entirely.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    Two lessons, and the second one only arrived on a second reading.
    A model has two separate jobs, and passing one says nothing about the other.
    Ranking answers "who is riskiest?" Calibration answers "how likely is this, really?" AUC only audits
    the first. Any decision that multiplies a probability by money depends entirely on the second.
    A comparison is a claim, and it needs the same scrutiny as a model. I built a
    careful model, corrected a serious scaling error, and then evaluated five programs against a baseline
    that couldn't support the conclusion I drew from it. The modeling was the easy part. Deciding what
    two numbers mean when you put them side by side is where the actual reasoning lives.

      Probability calibration

title: The sure thing problem
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  The sure thing problem
  
    A mobile game had proof its ads worked — conversion more than doubled in a clean
    experiment. The harder question was who to keep showing them to. Ranking players by who
    was most likely to buy turned out to be the expensive answer.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseMobile game ad targeting
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm · scikit-learn
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The setup
    A studio behind a successful mobile action game launched its first paid expansion at
    $14.99. Two months in, only 5.75% of active players had bought it.
    Leadership saw two possible explanations: the price was too high, or players simply didn't know the
    expansion existed.
    Cutting price is close to irreversible, so the awareness theory got tested first — with in-app
    ads. Showing a player ads for two weeks costs about $1.50 in forgone in-game
    currency purchases. That gives the whole problem a clean economic spine: an ad is worth showing
    only when it moves someone across the line by more than $1.50 ÷ $14.99, or about
    10 percentage points of purchase probability.
  

  
    The experiment worked. That was the easy part.
    Two randomly assigned groups of 30,000 players each — one saw ads, one didn't:
  

  
    5.69%Conversion without ads
    13.04%Conversion with ads
    +7.36ppAbsolute lift
    +129%Relative lift
  

  
    Before trusting any of that, I checked the randomization held. Average player level came in at
    6.22 versus 6.32 between groups; friend counts at 49.8 versus 51.0; spaceship ownership 71.5%
    versus 70.3%. Every feature landed inside a few percent. The groups were comparable, so the gap in
    conversion is the ads and not the players.

    
      Ads work on average. But you don't run a campaign on an average — you run it on a
      list. Averages hide the fact that a single number is hiding four completely different kinds of
      player.
    
  

  
    Four kinds of player
    Every player falls into one of four boxes, depending on what they'd do with the ad and what
    they'd do without it. Only one box is worth paying for.
  

  
    
      
        Who is actually worth $1.50?
        Select a group to see what targeting it does to the campaign. Conceptual
        framing — not measured segment sizes.
      
    
    ↓ Buys when shown an ad  ·  → Buys when shown nothing
    
      
        Sure ThingsBuys either way
      
        PersuadablesBuys only if shown the ad
      
        Sleeping DogsBuys only if left alone
      
        Lost CausesNever buys
    
    
  

  
    A propensity model ranks players by P(buy | ad). That score is high for Persuadables —
    but it's just as high for Sure Things, who were going to buy anyway. Spend $1.50 on a Sure Thing and
    you bought a conversion you already had.
    An uplift model ranks by the difference instead: P(buy | ad) − P(buy | no ad). Sure Things
    score near zero, because the ad changes nothing for them. Only Persuadables rise to the top.
  

  
    What the models actually returned
    I built both approaches — propensity and uplift — across four algorithms, then measured
    incremental profit on an 18,000-player holdout, scaled to the full 120,000-player base.
    The toggle below is the finding. It switches between sending ads to a fixed top 25% of players,
    and letting each model choose its own depth using the $1.50 ÷ $14.99 threshold.
  

  
    
      
        Incremental profit by model and targeting strategy
        
      
      
        Optimal depth
        Fixed 25%
      
    
    
      Propensity targeting
      Uplift targeting
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Model
Propensity
Uplift
Difference






    
    ≈ Values recorded to five significant figures in the original
    output; the logistic pair and all differences are exact.
  

  
    At a fixed 25%, the story looks inconsistent. The three flexible models show
    uplift winning by $735K–$783K. Logistic regression does the opposite — its uplift version returns
    $657,986 against $1,546,217 for propensity, an $888,231 loss. Read that column alone and uplift modeling looks
    unreliable.
    Let each model pick its own depth and the contradiction disappears. Uplift wins for all
    four, logistic included, by $386K to $499K. The best combination — gradient boosting on
    uplift scores, 30% of players — returns $2,893,786.

    
      The logistic anomaly was never really about logistic regression. It was about forcing every
      model to target the same 25%. Depth was a free parameter I'd accidentally frozen, and freezing it
      produced a finding that wasn't there.
    

    There's a second pattern worth noticing. Propensity models want a wider audience — their optima
    land at 30% to 40% — while uplift models converge tightly on 25% to 30%. Uplift makes more money
    while mailing fewer people, which is what you'd expect once Sure Things stop occupying slots at the
    top of the list.
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    How the uplift score is built
    
    I used the two-model approach. One model is fit on the treated group and one on the control
    group, using the same feature set — telemetry like level reached, days active, friend count, prior
    purchases, badges earned, and device type. Each player in the holdout gets scored by both.
    The uplift score is the difference between those two predictions. Propensity is just the first
    prediction on its own. Both rankings come from the same fitted models, so the comparison isolates
    the ranking rule rather than confounding it with model quality.
    The known weakness: subtracting two estimates adds their errors. When both models are noisy, the
    difference is noisier than either — which is exactly why the linear model struggled at fixed depth
    while the flexible models didn't.
    
    

    
    Where the 10.01% threshold comes from
    
    Showing ads costs $1.50; a conversion is worth $14.99. Targeting a player pays off when expected
    incremental revenue clears the cost:
    uplift × $14.99 > $1.50, so uplift > 0.1001
    Count how many holdout players clear that bar and you get the optimal depth directly from the
    data rather than from a round number. Those counts came to 24.23% for logistic uplift, 31.26% for
    the neural network, 31.46% for random forest, and 31.14% for gradient boosting — each rounded to the
    nearest 5% for a deployable rule.
    The same threshold applies to propensity scores, but it means something different there: it asks
    whether someone is likely to buy at all, not whether the ad is what moved them. Same arithmetic,
    different question — and that difference is the entire post.
    
    

    
    Validating the implementation across two libraries
    
    I built every model twice — once through the course's pyrsm wrapper, once directly
    in scikit-learn — then correlated the predictions to check the pipeline.
    Random forest agreed almost perfectly (0.999 on treatment predictions, 0.995 on uplift), and
    gradient boosting nearly as closely (0.975 / 0.979). The neural network came in far lower, at 0.595
    and 0.541.
    That gap isn't a bug — neural networks are sensitive to initialization, solver, and learning-rate
    schedule, and the two libraries don't share defaults. But it is a caution: the neural network's
    numbers are the least reproducible in the set, and I'd want a fixed seed and a matched optimizer
    before putting weight on them.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Report a range, not a point. Every profit figure is a single draw on one 18,000-row
    holdout. Two of the four differences fall within a few hundred thousand dollars of each other on a
    $2.8M base. Bootstrapped intervals would show which gaps survive resampling — my guess is the
    uplift-versus-propensity gap does, and the ranking among the three flexible models does not.
    Check the Sleeping Dogs empirically. The framing above assumes they exist, but I
    never tested the bottom of the uplift distribution for genuinely negative treatment effects. If ads
    actively suppress purchases for some players, that's a finding worth having on its own.
    Model the depth decision directly. Rounding 31.14% to 30% is defensible, but the
    profit curve near the optimum is flat enough that the rounding could matter more than the model
    choice. I'd plot profit across every decile before committing.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    The transferable lesson isn't "use uplift models." It's that the metric you rank on
    encodes a causal claim, whether or not you meant to make one. Ranking by who will
    convert quietly assumes the treatment caused the conversion. Ranking by who will convert
    because of the ad makes that assumption explicit and testable.
    The second lesson is cheaper to state and easier to forget: a comparison is only as honest as the
    parameters you held fixed. I nearly drew a conclusion about logistic regression that was
    really a conclusion about my own choice of 25%.

title: Curiosities thatshow up in my work.
text:
Hobbies
  Curiosities thatshow up in my work.
  
    These aren't unrelated to the analytical work — they're where I practice noticing
    patterns without a spreadsheet in front of me.
  

  
    
      Cooking & baking
      
        I’ve been cooking and baking since sixth grade, and I’m still always trying new restaurants and dishes around San Diego. Cooking has taught me that small details—timing, consistency, and careful adjustments—can change the entire result. I bring that same attention to my data work, whether I’m validating an output, cleaning a dataset, or finding a better solution when the original request is not possible. Some of my favorite spots are Seneca, Callie, Taco Stand, Din Tai Fung, and Ramen Nagi.
      
    
    
      Reading
      
        I am drawn to fiction and mysteries because I enjoy following scattered clues until they form a clear story. That same instinct shows up in my analytical work: I like taking information that feels disconnected or complicated and structuring it into something understandable, useful, and easy for others to follow.
      
    
    
      Art & sketching
      
        My background in studio art taught me to look at something from different angles and imagine how it could work better. I often carry that mindset into my work by quietly redesigning inefficient processes, improving how information is organized, or creating a more intuitive way for someone to complete a task.
      
    
    
      Gaming
      
        Games have taught me to stay patient with difficult problems, test different approaches, and keep going until I find a way forward. I care about completing the full experience—not just getting to the end, but making sure everything works as expected. That persistence shows up in how I troubleshoot, quality-check, and deliver analytical work.
